messages.subject: Spatial and Temporal replication
messages.body_plain:
I am working with a pretty standard point-count occupancy data set:  I
have 232 sites that were surveyed between 1 and 5 times in one
season.  (single-season, closed).  These sites are then distributed
across 108 patches of habitat with 1 - 7(or so) sites per patch.  Two
of my covariates are specific to the patch (patch area and patch
isolation), but then two of them are specific to the site/point (basal
area and grass cover).  I have successfully fitted models using the
site as the experimental unit, but there are issues with independence
between sites for the patch-level covariates.  I am wondering if there
is a way to set this up in an unmarked frame with a different
experimental unit for different covariates (like a split-plot
design).

My only thought so far is that each spatial/temporal replicate
combination is one actual replicate.  So that say one patch had 3
sites within it, two of the sites were sampled 4 times, and the third
was sampled 3 times.  then the experimental unit would be the patch
with 11 replicates,  averaging the site-level covariates across those
11 replicates.  This method is straightforward but some information is
lost.  If there is a way to accommodate this split-plot type design
please let me know.  Any advice would be appreciated.

Thanks,

Paul Taillie
North Carolina State University

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Estimates with linearComb
messages.body_plain:
Dear Aude,

you can get estimates from the model by hand or use the functionality of unmarked.

(a) You can type plogis(X) for a logit-scale parameter or prediction X (for occupancy or detection) to backtransform it from the logit to the probability scale. This will however not give you a SE or confidence interval
(b) For a "Null model", with just an intercept in the state and the detection model (i.e., for the model you imagine), you can use backTransform(), which will also yield a SE.
(c) For models with covariates, use predict, which will also yield SEs and 95% CIs.

Check the vignettes that come with unmarked. There is information on this in "Overview of unmarked" and also "Dynamic occupancy models in unmarked". Both are relevant for your occupancy model.

Regards  --  Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm currently researching various methods for modeling my data (see
below), and it seems like the N-mixture model with a ZIP distribution
for abundance (using 'unmarked' pcount() function) is the most
appropriate, given the source of zeros; however, before I dive in,
there is one issue I'm stuck on:

My data set consists of A) counts of shorebirds during winter (3 to 6
counts per winter, maximum 1 per month) at >150 coastal sites and B)
shoreline units for our entire study region, each characterized by
substrate type, exposure, and other environmental attributes. The goal
of our project is to 1) model the relationship between the abundance
of shorebirds and shoreline characteristics, and 2) to estimate the
total abundance of each shorebird species within the entire study
region based on these relationships.

I've been reading through the relevant literature and noticed in both
a thread in this forum and in a paper by Joseph et al. (2009) that
"the abundance estimates produced by N-mixture models are estimates of
the number of species that UTILIZE a site, rather than the true
density". This is particularly true if the birds are not always
available to be detected - which I believe to be true for shorebirds.

Is there a way to use the N-mixture model to estimate total abundance
across the species' distribution then? From what I understand, it
sounds like the predict() function will overestimate abundance in this
case.

Please let me know if anything is unclear - while I'm not new to R or
mixed-effects models, I am somewhat new to N-Mixture with zero-
inflation, and particularly using these models for prediction.

Thanks!

Cheers,
Jenn

Hi,

I'm currently researching various methods for modeling my data (see
below), and it seems like the N-mixture model with a ZIP distribution
for abundance (using 'unmarked' pcount() function) is the most
appropriate, given the source of zeros; however, before I dive in,
there is one issue I'm stuck on:

My data set consists of A) counts of shorebirds during winter (3 to 6
counts per winter, maximum 1 per month) at >150 coastal sites and B)
shoreline units for our entire study region, each characterized by
substrate type, exposure, and other environmental attributes. The goal
of our project is to 1) model the relationship between the abundance
of shorebirds and shoreline characteristics, and 2) to estimate the
total abundance of each shorebird species within the entire study
region based on these relationships.

I've been reading through the relevant literature and noticed in both
a thread in this forum and in a paper by Joseph et al. (2009) that
"the abundance estimates produced by N-mixture models are estimates of
the number of species that UTILIZE a site, rather than the true
density". This is particularly true if the birds are not always
available to be detected - which I believe to be true for shorebirds.

Is there a way to use the N-mixture model to estimate total abundance
across the species' distribution then? From what I understand, it
sounds like the predict() function will overestimate abundance in this
case.

Please let me know if anything is unclear - while I'm not new to R or
mixed-effects models, I am somewhat new to N-Mixture with zero-
inflation, and particularly using these models for prediction.

Thanks!

Cheers,
Jenn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Aude,

if you want to characterise the average occupancy probability and the average detection probability, then this approach is fine, what concerns the mean. However, for the standard error you would have to use the delta rule: you can't simply average the standard errors !

An alternative would be to fit the mean-centered covariates, in which case the intercept would represent the logit-scale occupancy and detection values for a typical covariate value, namely the mean of the observed values. You could then directly backtransform that to get both the estimate at the probability scale and its uncertainty (SE).

Centering covariates is very useful for interpretation of regression relationships, because it makes the intercept directly interpretable, something it is usually not, when it means the value of the response at a value of x=0.

Regards  ---  Marc

messages.subject: parboot() and parallel processing
messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked users,

I am curious if any among you have experience or tips you might be
able to share with respect to parsing a parboot() run to multiple
processor cores, particularly on a Windows based machine?

I have a double-observer pcount() model with 13 primary occasions in
which approximately 150 locations were sampled each time.  The 150
sites are delineated into 7 stream segments, and by modeling abundance
as time dependent (primary occasion) with an interaction between
stream segment plus four additional habitat covariates, I end up with
more than 100 parameter estimates for the full model.  The data are
overdispersed, and I'm wanting to use parboot() to estimate the
dispersion, so I can then rank models by QAIC.

The problem is that the full pcount() model takes about 10 hrs to fit
on my Core2Duo desktop (3.2GB RAM), and experience has shown (with
simpler models) that the length of time to complete a single parboot()
iteration can vary considerably depending on the particular dataset
generated for a given simulation run.  I've benchmarked some pcount()
model fitting run times on various machines, including one in my
laboratory with dual Xeon processors and 16GB of RAM, as will was a 20
core (7GB RAM) Amazon EC2 machine on the "cloud", which both decreased
the processing time by about 20%.

I've tested the "boot()" example from the "parallel" R package and I
am able to generate 1000 runs by bootstrapping 500 simulations to each
of the two processors on my desktop.  The example I used from the
documentation is this:

> run1 <- function(...) {
+ library(boot)
+ cd4.rg <- function(data, mle) MASS::mvrnorm(nrow(data), mle$m, mle
$v)
+ cd4.mle <- list(m = colMeans(cd4), v = var(cd4))
+ boot(cd4, corr, R = 500, sim = "parametric",
+ ran.gen = cd4.rg, mle = cd4.mle)
+ }
>mc<- 2
> cl <- makeCluster(mc)
> ## make this reproducible
> clusterSetRNGStream(cl, 123)
> library(boot) # needed for c() method on master
> cd4.boot <- do.call(c, parLapply(cl, seq_len(mc), run1) )
> boot.ci <http://boot.ci>(cd4.boot, type = c("norm", "basic", "perc"),
+ conf = 0.9, h = atanh, hinv = tanh)
> stopCluster(cl)

I've tried to expand upon this example to get parboot() to run
similarly on multiple cores.  Ideally, for example, I'd like to send
one parboot simulation run for my full model to each of 20 cores on an
Amazon EC2 machine which might then yield 20 parboot() simulation runs
in about 10 hours (plus or minus).  If I repeated this on n machines I
could theoretically obtain 20n parboot() runs in about a 10 hour
period.

Thus far, none of my implementations have worked.  I think I was close
on a recent attempt, but I believe the two cores on my desktop might
have been stomping on eachother with simultaneous requests to access
the stored pcount() model object.

Apologies in advance for my lack of tech savvy computer lingo, or my
poor modeling jargon-- I am still learning much in both departments.
That said, I am grateful for the informative discussions I've learned
from here.

Any ideas greatly appreciated.

Kind regards, Ted Jones

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ted,

The Royle (Biometrics 2004) N-mixture model assumes population closure (ie 1 primary period) so I don't see how you could model abundance as time-dependent. Have you looked at pcountOpen, which fits the open-population model of Dail and Madsen (Biometrics 2011)?  Also, have you considered directly modeling overdispersion using the negative bionomial or ZIP distributions?

To run parboot on multiple cores, you could do something like this:

library(unmarked)
library(parallel)
example(parboot)

cl <- makeCluster(getOption("cl.cores", 2))
clusterExport(cl, c("fm", "fitstats"))
clusterSetRNGStream(cl, 123)

sims <- clusterEvalQ(cl, {
    library(unmarked)
    parboot(fm, fitstats, nsim=20)
})
str(sims)

stopCluster(cl)

Hope this helps.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Many thanks for the reply, Richard

Your easy to follow example appears to be working!

Looking forward to testing it on the Amazon Cloud (and possibly seeing
a parboot run of 100 or more sometime before next year).

Regarding the N-mixture model, I am aware of the closure assumption,
and considered the Dail-Madsen open model.  However, to keep things
simple, I used the Royle (2004) pcount model by assigning primary
occasion (bi-monthly sample) as a factor, and I assume the change in
abundance between occasions represents the balance of recruitment/
mortality/movement that occurs in the bi-monthly interim between
primary occasions.

On a side note, the assumption of closure for populations at the site-
level is not perfectly met at the secondary occasion level for my
data.  There is some small amount of movement by individuals among
trap sites during a double-sample, although movement between stream
segments is unlikely during the two consecutive samples which occur on
back-to-back days.  I believe the movement among trap sites may be
partially responsible for the excessive dispersion (2 < c-hat < 4,
likely).

I tried both NB and ZIP distributions as well.  For the NB models, I
observed the same phenomenon of increasing lamda and decreasing p,
when walking K upward, to the point where the estimates become very
unrealistic.  I am not entirely interested in estimating total
abundance per se, because it is not entirely clear what the sampling
universe is (ie, the universe defined by the range of trap influence),
especially in light of the potential for movement between trap sites
during a double-sample.  Instead, I'm using the model to more
generally infer about the relationship between abundance and habitat.

The webinar, this discussion board, and several great papers like the
Royle (2004) and the Dail and Madsen (2011) papers you mentioned, have
helped make the learning curve much less steep.

Thanks again,

Ted

messages.subject: Occupancy data for diversity indices
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

There's been some discussion about using Unmarked for estimating species richness, but I wanted to bounce an alternative approach off the group.  I'd like to use occupancy data to calculate Shannon-Weiner diversity indices (i.e., accounting for species evenness in addition to richness). The idea would be to:
1) use pcount to estimate local abundance of each species at each sampling site
2) use those estimates to calculate predicted diversity at each site
3) determine which covariates are related to variation in diversity among sites.

My question is this: at what point should the covariates be entered into the analysis?  I can see two potential strategies:

A) The covariates are entered at step 1 by being incorporated into the abundance function in pcount. But then when data from multiple species are "pooled" into the diversity index, how would I assess the effects of each covariate on overall diversity?  One option would be to just look at the R-squared value of simple relationships between diversity and each covariate individually.

B) I could use ranef() in step 1 to generate site-specific abundance estimates for each species without accounting for any covariates, then calculate site-specific diversity, then run regression models to see how overall diversity is related to the covariates, individually and jointly.

What would people think of the validity of either of these approaches, or are there any better suggestions out there?

Many thanks in advance.

messages.body_plain:
hi Kristen,

as Andy says, it is not a problem, neither for a model for abundance, nor for one of occupancy. Indeed, this is one of the great benefits of a modeling framework that separately models the state and the observation processes, that effects of a single covariate on both model components can be teased apart.

BTW, it is easy to convince yourself of this by quickly simulating data and then analysing them. Below is a function to generate data from a particularly ugly system: where the effects of a single covariate partly cancel each other out in the observed counts.

Regards  --  Marc

# Define function for generating binomial-mix model data

data.fn <- function(R = 200, T = 3, xmin = -1, xmax = 1, alpha0 = 1, alpha1 = 3, beta0 = 0, beta1 = -5){

# R: number of sites at which counts were made (= number of spatial reps)

# T: number of times that counts were made at each site
# (= number of temporal reps)

# xmin, xmax: define range of the covariate X

# alpha0 and alpha1: intercept and slope of log-linear regression
# relating abundance to the site covariate A

# beta0 and beta1: intercept and slope of logistic-linear regression
# of detection probability on A

   y <- array(dim = c(R, T)) # Array for counts

   # Ecological process

   # Covariate values: sort for ease of presentation

   X <- sort(runif(n = R, min = xmin, max = xmax))

   # Relationship expected abundance – covariate

   lam <- exp(alpha0 + alpha1 * X)

   # Add Poisson noise: draw N from Poisson(lambda)

   N <- rpois(n = R, lambda = lam)

   table(N)                # Distribution of abundances across sites

   sum(N > 0) / R          # Empirical occupancy

   totalN <- sum(N)  ;  totalN

   # Observation process

   # Relationship detection prob – covariate

   p <- plogis(beta0 + beta1 * X)

   # Make a ‘census’ (i.e., go out and count things)

   for (i in 1:T){

      y[,i] <- rbinom(n = R, size = N, prob = p)

      }

   # Naïve regression

   naive.pred <- exp(predict(glm(apply(y, 1, max) ~ X + I(X^2), family =   poisson)))

   # Plot features of the simulated system

   par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

   plot(X, lam, main = "Expected abundance", xlab = "Covariate", ylab = "lambda", las = 1, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 3, frame.plot = FALSE)

   plot(X, N, main = "Realised abundance", xlab = "Covariate", ylab = "N", las = 1, frame.plot = FALSE, col = "red", cex = 1.2)

   plot(X, p, ylim = c(0, 1), main = "Detection probability", xlab = "Covariate", ylab = "p", type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 3, las = 1, frame.plot = FALSE)

   plot(X, naive.pred, main = "Actual counts \n and naïve regression", xlab = "Covariate", ylab = "Relative abundance", ylim = c(min(y), max(y)), type = "l", lty = 2, lwd = 4, col = "blue", las = 1, frame.plot = FALSE)

points(rep(X, T), y, col = "black", cex = 1.2)

   # Return stuff

   return(list(R = R, T = T, X = X, alpha0 = alpha0, alpha1 = alpha1, beta0 = beta0, beta1 = beta1, lam = lam, N = N, totalN = totalN, p = p, y = y))

   }

To execute, do this:

data <- data.fn()

Hello all,

   I am establishing line transects that we will drive with a vehicle and 2 observers to estimate ungulate abundance across a landscape with varying types of habitat (open grasslands to dense woodland).  A permanent river bisects the study area.  We want to use habitat and distance to river as transect-level covariates.  I have established 10 straight-line transects in GIS, varying in length from 4 - 25 km, but I hope to partition these into shorter sampling units based on habitat type and distance to river for analysis.  I have a few questions about how to set up the transects to analyze the data in distsamp.  These are kind of survey design questions with an objective of using distsamp.  Hope this is appropriate...

1) Can I subdivide each of the 10 transects by habitat type and use each of these as a 'transect'?  For example, say I have a 4 km east to west transect, which is composed of 1 km riparian, 2 km grassland, and 1 km bushland.  I would prefer to analyze these as 3 separate, but contiguous, transects, but was concerned about issues of spatial autocorrelation.  Any suggestions of how to account for this in distsamp?

2) In some areas, we may have to meander away from a perfect straight line transect, making more of a curved transect.  Though we will not be following an established road, we will be using a path of lesser resistance.  I am trying to decide what would be an appropriate method to calculate the perpendicular distance from the transect.  Hiby and Krishna (2001) calculated the distance to the nearest portion of the curve.  We were considering taking the vehicle's bearing, the bearing of the animals, and the sighting distance to calculate the perpendicular distance from our point on the curve.  I'd be interested in any suggestions any of you might have.

3) Any plans for multi-season distsamp models?  We plan to continue our animal counts every 8 weeks for 3 years.  I could do multiple, single-season analyses, but thought I'd ask out of curiosity.

Thanks again for developing these models and putting together great manuals, forums, and workshops.  I just received news that one of my multi-season occupancy modeling papers using the colext model was accepted for publication.  More details to come soon!  Thanks for your help.
